reasoning: The core problem — how much an authority/expert/confidence provenance cue increases a judge's acceptance of (incorrect) content when the answer text is held fixed — is directly studied. "Trust Me, I'm an Expert" (arXiv 2601.13433) holds content constant, varies expert vs non-expert source labels, quantifies the authority-deference effect, and tests a debiasing/steering mitigation. "Justice or Prejudice? (CALM)" (arXiv 2410.02736) explicitly includes an "authority bias" attack on LLM judges, adding fabricated authoritative references to an inferior answer and showing the judge flips to accept it; "The Silent Judge" and judge-bias surveys cover the same provenance/shortcut biases plus prompt-instruction debiasing (which is reported to often fail against strong cues). Sycophancy work further establishes the magnitude of authority-cue effects (e.g., accuracy dropping from 45% to ~1% under authoritative framing). The proposal's specific four-way framing (neutral/expert/verified/low-confidence draft) on weak-judge oversight QA with a simple system-prompt debiaser is a minor recombination of these existing contributions rather than an unexplored gap, so the gaps are minor.

evidence.title: Trust Me, I'm an Expert: Decoding and Steering Authority Bias in Large Language Models
evidence.summary: Holds content constant while varying expert vs non-expert source/endorsement labels to quantify authority bias (how much an expert attribution increases acceptance of identical content). Also tests mitigation via steering vectors / debiasing, directly matching the proposal's hold-answer-fixed + debias design.

evidence.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM)
evidence.summary: Explicitly defines and attacks 'authority bias' in LLM judges by adding fabricated authoritative references to a lower-quality answer; shows judges reverse to accept the inferior/incorrect answer and even cite the fake references. Covers the judge-oversight acceptance-of-wrong-answer angle.

evidence.title: The Silent Judge: Unacknowledged Shortcut Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
evidence.summary: Studies shortcut/provenance biases in LLM judges including authority and confidence cues; establishes that provenance labels impose a trust hierarchy (EXPERT > HUMAN > LLM > UNKNOWN) and that judges accept content based on framing rather than correctness.

evidence.title: Evaluating and Mitigating LLM-as-a-judge Bias in Communication Systems
evidence.summary: Surveys and tests prompt-based debiasing instructions (e.g., instructing the judge to ignore tone/identity/source cues) as mitigation for judge biases, and notes such instruction-only debiasing often fails against strong bias injections — directly addressing the proposal's debiasing-instruction question.

evidence.title: Impact of authoritative and subjective cues on large language model reliability for clinical inquiries
evidence.summary: Experimental study showing authoritative framing dramatically degrades correctness (accuracy dropping from ~45% to ~1% under authoritative prompts), quantifying the magnitude of the authority-deference effect on held-fixed factual content.

evidence.title: When Truth Is Overridden / Decomposing Factual Sycophancy
evidence.summary: Studies authority/expertise cues driving models to abandon correct internal knowledge (sycophancy), with a finding that stated expertise has smaller effect than opinion expression — relevant nuance to the proposed authority-vs-confidence comparison.
